A social messaging company is building an AI chat assistant using Amazon Bedrock. The company must ensure that every inference complies with an approved safety policy. Specifically, the company wants to:  
  
- Block harmful prompts before model invocations  
- Filter streamed model outputs in real time  
- Route flagged cases for human review  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure an AWS Step Functions workflow. Configure a step to use an AWS Lambda function to pre-check inputs by using the ApplyGuardrail API. Use an InvokeModelWithResponseStream API step that has the guardrail attached. Configure a second Lambda function step to post-check outputs by using the ApplyGuardrail API. Route flagged items to an Amazon SQS queue. Enforce guardrail use by using a bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier IAM condition.

Configure an AWS Step Functions workflow. Configure a step to call the ApplyGuardrail API before inference. Then call the InvokeModel API without streaming and use the guardrail. Store the results in Amazon S3. Use the client UI to hide problematic tokens.

Configure an AWS Step Functions workflow. Configure a step to use the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API that has the guardrail attached for in-stream filtering. Run an AWS Lambda post-check step by using the ApplyGuardrail API to check flagged cases. Do not perform pre-inference.

Configure an AWS Step Functions workflow that includes steps to perform pre-checks and post-checks by using the ApplyGuardrail API and the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API. Attach the guardrail to the check steps. Use process controls such as code reviews instead of IAM enforcement to ensure that guardrails are always applied.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Bedrock's ApplyGuardrail API can independently evaluate INPUT text (prompts) before a model is invoked and OUTPUT text (model responses) after generation, without requiring a model call — making it suitable for both a pre-inference block of harmful prompts and a post-inference check of generated content. Attaching a guardrail directly to the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API enables real-time filtering of streamed tokens as they are generated. Routing guardrail-flagged content to a queue such as Amazon SQS enables asynchronous human review of borderline or blocked cases. To guarantee that every inference request actually uses the approved guardrail (rather than relying on developers to remember to specify it), Bedrock supports the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier IAM condition key, which can be enforced in an IAM policy attached to the InvokeModel/InvokeModelWithResponseStream/Converse/ConverseStream actions; any request lacking or mismatching the required guardrail identifier is denied. This combination — Step Functions orchestrating Lambda pre-check (ApplyGuardrail), streaming inference with an attached guardrail, Lambda post-check (ApplyGuardrail), SQS routing for review, and IAM-based enforcement — comprehensively satisfies all stated requirements.

**Learn more:** [Enforce the use of specific guardrails in model inference requests - Amazon Bedrock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-permissions-id.html) · [Use the ApplyGuardrail API in your application - Amazon Bedrock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-use-independent-api.html)

A company built a multimodal content-analysis application on Amazon Bedrock. The application routes different content types (text, images, and code) to specialized foundation models (FMs).  
  
The application must handle multiple types of routing decisions:  
  
- Simple routing based on file extension must have minimal latency.  
- Complex routing based on content semantics requires analysis before FM selection.  
- The application must provide detailed history and support fallback options when primary FMs fail.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure AWS Lambda functions that call Amazon Bedrock FMs for all routing logic. Use conditional statements to determine the appropriate FM based on content type and semantics.

Create a hybrid solution. Handle simple routing based on file extensions in application code. Handle complex content-based routing by using an AWS Step Functions state machine with JSONata for content analysis and the InvokeModel API for specialized FMs.

Deploy separate AWS Step Functions workflows for each content type with routing logic in AWS Lambda functions. Use Amazon EventBridge to coordinate between workflows when fallback to alternate FMs is required.

Use Amazon SQS with different SQS queues for each content type. Configure AWS Lambda consumers that analyze content and invoke appropriate FMs based on message attributes by using Amazon Bedrock with an AWS SDK.

questions.explanation:
A hybrid approach best fits the differing needs of the two routing scenarios. Handling extension-based routing directly in application code avoids the overhead of an orchestration service call, keeping latency minimal for the simple case. For complex, semantics-driven routing, an AWS Step Functions state machine can use JSONata expressions to analyze and transform the content/state data before selecting a model, then invoke the chosen specialized FM through the Bedrock optimized service integration (the InvokeModel API action, arn:aws:states:::bedrock:invokeModel). Step Functions state machines inherently log every state transition, giving detailed execution history, and support built-in Retry and Catch error-handling constructs, which provide automatic fallback to alternate FMs when a primary model invocation fails. This combination — lightweight code-based routing for the simple case and a Step Functions/JSONata/InvokeModel workflow for the complex case — satisfies all the stated latency, analysis, auditability, and fallback requirements.

**Learn more:** [Invoke and customize Amazon Bedrock models with Step Functions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-bedrock.html) · [AWS Step Functions Developer Guide - Error handling in Step Functions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/concepts-error-handling.html)

A company is building a multicloud generative AI (GenAI)-powered secret resolution application that uses Amazon Bedrock and Agent Squad. The application resolves secrets from multiple sources, including key stores and hardware security modules (HSMs), using AWS Lambda functions to retrieve the secrets.  
  
The application has the following characteristics:  
  
- Uses AWS AppConfig to implement dynamic feature gating  
- Supports secret chaining and detects secret drift  
- Handles short-lived and expiring secrets  
- Supports prompt flows for templated instructions  
- Uses AWS Step Functions to orchestrate agents that resolve secrets and manage secret validation and drift detection  
  
During testing, the company identifies the following issues:  
  
- The application does not refresh expired secrets in time for agents to use them  
- The application sends alerts for secret drift, but agents continue to use stale data  
- Prompt flows within the application reuse outdated templates, causing cascading failures  
  
The company must resolve these performance issues.  
  
Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Use Step Functions Map states to run agent workflows in parallel. Pass updated secret metadata through Lambda function outputs. Use AWS AppConfig to version all prompt flows to gate and roll back faulty templates.
Use Amazon Bedrock AgentCore only. Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails to restrict prompt variation. Use an inline JSON schema for a single agent’s workflow definition to chain tool calls.
Use a centralized Amazon EventBridge pipeline to invoke each event agent. Store intermediate prompts in Amazon DynamoDB. Resolve agent ordering by using TTL-based backoff and retries.

Use Amazon EventBridge Pipes to invoke resolvers based on Amazon CloudWatch log patterns. Store response metadata in Amazon DynamoDB. Configure a TTL and versioned writes. Use Amazon Q Developer to dynamically generate fallback prompts that are routed through a Lambda coordinator.

questions.explanation:
Step Functions Map states let agent workflows run concurrently instead of sequentially, eliminating the delay that prevents expired secrets from being refreshed in time. Passing updated secret metadata directly through Lambda function outputs (rather than relying solely on drift alerts) ensures agents actually consume the refreshed values instead of stale data. Versioning prompt flow templates in AWS AppConfig, and using AppConfig's feature-gating/rollback capability, prevents agents from reusing outdated templates and lets the company quickly roll back a faulty template before it causes cascading failures. This approach extends the already-adopted AWS-native orchestration stack (Step Functions, Lambda, AppConfig) rather than replacing it with unrelated services.

**Learn more:** [Using Map state in Distributed mode for large-scale parallel workloads in Step Functions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-map-distributed.html) · [AWS AppConfig feature flags and dynamic configuration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appconfig/latest/userguide/what-is-appconfig.html)

The job output, including the evaluation report, is written to a specified S3 location. Running a separate evaluation job for each candidate FM, with that FM designated as the generator, produces automated comparative reports for the data scientist. QuickSight is not a supported output target for Bedrock evaluation jobs, and assigning the FM under test as the 'evaluator' (rather than generator) is incorrect, since the judge model performs the scoring, not the model being tested.

Sending requests to an Amazon SQS queue and processing them with AWS Fargate decouples the ingestion layer from the compute layer, enabling the system to absorb sudden traffic spikes and scale the processing tier independently and resiliently. Invoking the small, low-latency model first and only forwarding low-confidence results (score below 0.65) to a second SQS queue for asynchronous processing by the larger model ensures the expensive model is invoked only when necessary, directly optimizing cost while still allowing high-confidence results to be handled quickly. Amazon Bedrock's ApplyGuardrail API can independently evaluate INPUT text (prompts) before a model is invoked and OUTPUT text (model responses) after generation, without requiring a model call — making it suitable for both a pre-inference block of harmful prompts and a post-inference check of generated content. Attaching a guardrail directly to the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API enables real-time filtering of streamed tokens as they are generated. Routing guardrail-flagged content to a queue such as Amazon SQS enables asynchronous human review of borderline or blocked cases. To guarantee that every inference request actually uses the approved guardrail (rather than relying on developers to remember to specify it), Bedrock supports the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier IAM condition key, which can be enforced in an IAM policy attached to the InvokeModel/InvokeModelWithResponseStream/Converse/ConverseStream actions; any request lacking or mismatching the required guardrail identifier is denied. This combination — Step Functions orchestrating Lambda pre-check (ApplyGuardrail), streaming inference with an attached guardrail, Lambda post-check (ApplyGuardrail), SQS routing for review, and IAM-based enforcement — comprehensively satisfies all stated requirements.

A university is developing an AI-powered application composed of several sub-applications, including AI assistants, assignment graders, and internal analytics tools. The university is defining and testing multiple prompts across various foundation models (FMs) and wants to:  
  
- Compare variants of each prompt and select the variant that produces outputs best suited for each specific use case.  
- Implement version control for the prompts.  
- Test prompt variations and collect audit trails covering prompt changes and prompt usage.  
- Maintain consistency while still allowing the prompts to be integrated into the main application.  
  
Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to create versioned prompts. Include parameterized variables for each use case.
Store prompts in Amazon S3. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the model interactions and service integrations.
Use Amazon Bedrock Flows to create workflows that combine FMs and AWS services.
Configure AWS Config to record prompt changes. Use AWS CloudTrail to track prompt usage.
Configure Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management provides built-in prompt versioning and supports parameterized variables, enabling teams to create, test, and compare prompt variants for different use cases without building custom infrastructure. Because it is a native Bedrock feature, all prompt changes and invocations are automatically captured in AWS CloudTrail, satisfying the audit-trail requirement with no extra logging setup. Amazon Bedrock Flows allows prompts, FMs, and AWS service integrations to be composed into consistent, reusable workflows, making it straightforward to integrate versioned prompts into the university's main application and its various sub-applications. Together, these two fully managed Bedrock capabilities meet all stated requirements with minimal operational overhead, unlike custom solutions built on S3/Step Functions or manually configured AWS Config/CloudTrail tracking, and unlike intelligent prompt routing, which addresses model selection rather than versioning or auditing.

**Learn more:** [Manage prompts using Prompt management in Amazon Bedrock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html) · [Create your own generative AI workflows using Prompt Flows for Amazon Bedrock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/flows.html)

A financial services company is building a natural language processing (NLP) application that uses an AWS Lambda function to process customer trade inquiries using Amazon Bedrock foundation models (FMs). The Lambda function needs to generate comprehensive trade analysis responses that typically:  
  
- Exceed 4 MB in size  
- Require 15-20 seconds to complete  
  
The application must also:  
  
- Respond to customer inquiries in under 10 seconds  
- Comply with financial regulatory requirements to retain records for 10 years  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Implement response streaming to display partial responses as the application generates them. Set a 15-second timeout for Lambda function execution time. Enable AWS X-Ray tracing to monitor performance.
Use Amazon SQS queues to implement asynchronous invocations. Set a 30-second timeout for Lambda function execution time. Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor response times.

Use Amazon API Gateway to poll the application. Integrate the application with Amazon ElastiCache to cache responses. Set a 30-second timeout for Lambda function execution time. Collect detailed Amazon CloudWatch logs for application performance.
Implement response streaming to display partial responses as the application generates them. Set a 30-second timeout for Lambda function execution time. Store complete response records in Amazon S3.

questions.explanation:
Lambda response streaming allows the function to send partial output to the client as it is generated, so the customer starts receiving output well within the 10-second requirement even though full generation takes 15-20 seconds. A 30-second Lambda execution timeout ensures the function has enough time to finish generating the full 15-20 second response without being prematurely terminated (a 15-second timeout risks cutting off longer responses). Storing the complete response records in Amazon S3 provides durable, long-term storage suitable for meeting the 10-year regulatory retention requirement, which CloudWatch logs, X-Ray traces, or ElastiCache caching are not designed to satisfy.

A financial services company handles over 10,000 customer inquiries each day using a multi-agent GenAI application built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The agents in this application invoke several custom tools. During peak usage periods, users report that these custom tools experience failure rates as high as 40%, and the tools perform inconsistently across different teams within the company.  
  
A GenAI developer needs to implement an observability solution that delivers end-to-end visibility into agent interactions and tool behavior. The solution must:  
  
- Use built-in Amazon Bedrock capabilities  
- Not require custom instrumentation  
- Introduce minimal performance overhead  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable AgentCore Observability and trace collection. Use AWS X-Ray to capture distributed traces for the custom tools. Build Amazon CloudWatch dashboards to visualize metrics for errors, throttling, and latency during peak usage periods.

Use Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights to monitor the agents. Configure an AWS Lambda function to poll the Amazon Bedrock API for tool usage metrics. Configure the function to store results in CloudWatch to generate alerts.

Build a custom ETL pipeline that uses AWS Lambda functions to process Amazon CloudWatch logs from Amazon Bedrock. Store the processed data in Amazon DynamoDB. Use Amazon Quick Sight to visualize cross-team performance patterns.

Enable AgentCore Observability and send trace data to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use a custom AWS Lambda function to extract tool performance metrics from the logs. Use Amazon Managed Grafana to visualize trends.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability is a native, built-in capability that automatically emits OpenTelemetry-compatible traces, spans, metrics, and logs without requiring developers to write custom instrumentation code. AgentCore's built-in integration with AWS X-Ray provides distributed tracing by propagating trace context across service boundaries once observability and CloudWatch Transaction Search are enabled — this is a native setup step, not custom code. Amazon CloudWatch then natively provides observability dashboards and metrics (invocation counts, errors, throttling, latency) that can be used to visualize tool performance during peak periods across teams. This combination satisfies the requirements for built-in functionality, no custom instrumentation, end-to-end visibility, and minimal overhead. In contrast, solutions requiring custom Lambda functions to poll APIs or parse logs, custom ETL pipelines, or third-party visualization tools like Grafana or QuickSight introduce custom instrumentation and additional operational overhead that violate the stated constraints.

**Learn more:** [Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and AWS X-Ray](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services-agentcore.html) · [Observe your agent applications on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/observability.html)

The company plans to upgrade to a newer FM version but needs a validation system that can detect semantic drift in the assistant's responses, so that performance and functionality remain consistent for end users.  
  
The company needs a solution that can:  
  
- Compare responses between the current and new FM versions across 500 test cases  
- Detect changes in the meaning of responses  
- Generate quantitative similarity scores  
- Complete the validations  
- Log detailed results for historical comparison  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational complexity?

options.text: Configure Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canaries that use custom JavaScript code to send identical prompts to both new and existing FM versions. Store responses in Amazon S3. Perform manual reviews to identify semantic differences between FM versions.

Configure an AWS Step Functions workflow that sends test prompts to both new and existing FM versions. Use Amazon Bedrock embedding models to calculate cosine similarity scores. Store the results in Amazon DynamoDB with a composite key schema.

Use Amazon Bedrock model evaluation jobs to compare the new FM version against the current version using the 500 test cases. Configure the evaluation to calculate semantic similarity metrics. Store results in Amazon S3 for historical comparison.

Build a custom solution by using Amazon SageMaker AI to train a classifier model on historical responses to detect anomalies when the solution compares responses from the new FM version to previous patterns.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Bedrock model evaluation jobs are a built-in, fully managed feature designed exactly for this use case: comparing model outputs across a dataset of prompts, computing automatic metrics such as semantic similarity, and producing a report that can be stored in Amazon S3 for historical tracking. Because this capability is native to Bedrock, it requires no custom orchestration, embedding invocation code, database schema design, or model training, making it the lowest-operational-complexity option compared to building custom pipelines with Step Functions/DynamoDB, manual review workflows with CloudWatch Synthetics, or training a custom SageMaker anomaly-detection classifier.

- Customer purchase data from Amazon DynamoDB  
- Product reviews from Amazon S3  
- Customer profile information from Amazon RDS  
  
The function then sends this data directly to the Amazon Bedrock model through API calls. Recently, customers with extensive purchase histories have started receiving incomplete recommendations.  
  
Amazon CloudWatch logs for the Lambda function show execution timeouts, and CloudWatch logs for the Amazon Bedrock API calls show intermittent errors. Upon reviewing the logs, the company finds that some requests fail with context length exceeded errors, while other requests complete but appear to ignore portions of the input data.  
  
The company wants the recommendation system to take into account all customer data when generating recommendations, and it wants to use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to improve how the data is organized and retrieved.  
  
Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Implement a chunking strategy that divides the customer data into smaller segments. Configure the model to process each segment separately. Invoke the model a final time to synthesize the individual responses into comprehensive recommendations.

Modify the prompt structure to place the most critical information at the beginning and end of the context window. Implement token-counting logic to truncate less important data when the interaction approaches the model’s maximum context length.
Replace Claude Sonnet with a model that has a larger context window capacity. Increase the Lambda function timeout to accommodate longer processing times for larger inputs.
Configure the recommendation system to use the Converse API. Modify the additionalModelRequestFields parameter to increase the maximum token limit beyond the model’s default context window size.

Implement RAG by using a knowledge base to index the customer data with vector embeddings. Retrieve only the most semantically relevant information for each recommendation request based on the current customer context.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases enable a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pattern in which customer data is indexed as vector embeddings, allowing the system to retrieve only the most semantically relevant information for each recommendation request instead of forwarding the entire dataset into the model's context window. This resolves both the context length exceeded errors and the issue of the model ignoring portions of large inputs. Pairing this with a chunking strategy — splitting large customer data into smaller segments, processing each segment within the model's context limits, and then invoking the model once more to synthesize the partial outputs into a single comprehensive recommendation — ensures that no customer data, even for customers with extensive purchase histories, is dropped or truncated. Truncating data (as in option B) would violate the requirement to consider all customer data, and simply switching models or expanding token limits (options C and D) does not address the requirement to use Bedrock Knowledge Bases for better data organization and retrieval.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

questions.explanation:

A retail company operates an application that provides product recommendations to customers on its website. The application uses Amazon Bedrock to generate these recommendations by dynamically building prompts and sending them to foundation models (FMs).  
  
A GenAI developer deploys an update to the application that instructs the FM to include a specific promotional message whenever it generates a response to prompts. During testing, the developer finds that:  
  
- The promotional message does not always appear in the responses.  
- When the promotional message does appear, it does not always flow smoothly with the rest of the text.  
  
The GenAI developer needs to guarantee that the promotional message always appears in the FM's responses.  
  
Which solution meets this requirement?

options.text: Use an Amazon Bedrock Guardrails filter on the prompt. Set the input filter strength to HIGH.
Generate multiple response variants that include the promotional message in different ways. Use a reranker model to select the most coherent version based on relevance to the original prompt.

Run the prompt through Amazon Bedrock. Process the response through Amazon Bedrock Agents to add the promotional message. Rerank the results by using the original prompt and the desired message as context.
Reinforce the requirement to include the new promotional message within product recommendations by using an output indicator in prompts to the FM.

questions.explanation:
Prompt-only instructions to a foundation model are not deterministic — the model may omit the requested content or integrate it awkwardly. To guarantee that the promotional message is always present and reads naturally, the response must be processed after generation: run the prompt through Amazon Bedrock to get the initial recommendation, then use Amazon Bedrock Agents to programmatically insert the promotional message into the response (ensuring 100% inclusion), and rerank the result using the original prompt and the desired promotional message as context so the final text is coherent. This combination removes reliance on the FM's voluntary compliance with an embedded instruction and instead enforces the requirement architecturally, while still optimizing for natural flow.

**Learn more:** [How Amazon Bedrock Agents works](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-how.html) · [Use a reranker model in Amazon Bedrock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/rerank-use.html)

A company is building a generative AI (GenAI) application that uses Amazon Bedrock foundation models (FMs). The solution must meet the following requirements:  
  
- Authenticate users through Microsoft Entra ID.  
- Ensure that all foundation model (FM) API calls travel only over private network paths.  
- Restrict application access so that each department can use only specific model families.  
- Provide a comprehensive audit trail of all model interactions.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure SAML federation between Microsoft Entra ID and IAM. Create department-specific IAM roles that allow only the required ModelId values. Create AWS PrivateLink interface VPC endpoints for Amazon Bedrock runtime services. Enable AWS CloudTrail to capture Amazon Bedrock API calls. Configure Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to record detailed model interactions.

Create an identity provider (IdP) connection in IAM to authenticate by using Microsoft Entra ID. Assign department permission sets to control access to specific model families. Deploy AWS Lambda functions in private subnets with a NAT gateway for egress to Amazon Bedrock public endpoints. Enable CloudWatch Logs to capture model interactions for auditing purposes.

Create a SAML identity provider (IdP) in IAM to authenticate by using Microsoft Entra ID. Use IAM permissions boundaries to limit department roles’ access to specific model families. Configure public Amazon Bedrock API endpoints with VPC routing to maintain private network connectivity. Set up AWS CloudTrail with Amazon S3 Lifecycle rules to manage audit logs of model interactions.

Configure OpenID Connect (OIDC) federation between Microsoft Entra ID and IAM. Use attribute-based access control to map department attributes to specific model access permissions. Apply SCP policies to restrict access to Amazon Bedrock FM families based on department. Use Microsoft Entra ID’s built-in logging capabilities to maintain an audit trail of model interactions.

questions.explanation:
Federating Microsoft Entra ID with IAM through SAML lets users assume IAM roles based on their identity, and department-specific IAM roles can be scoped with policy conditions that permit only certain ModelId values, enforcing model-family restrictions per department. Creating AWS PrivateLink interface VPC endpoints for the Amazon Bedrock runtime service ensures that InvokeModel and related API calls travel entirely over the AWS private network rather than the public internet. For auditing, AWS CloudTrail records management and data events for Bedrock API calls (caller identity, modelId, timestamps), while Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging separately captures the full request and response payloads (prompts and completions) to Amazon S3/CloudWatch Logs — together these provide the comprehensive audit trail of model interactions that AWS documentation recommends for governance of Bedrock usage.

**Learn more:** [Implementing least privilege access for Amazon Bedrock](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/implementing-least-privilege-access-for-amazon-bedrock/) · [Configure model invocation logging in Amazon Bedrock by using AWS CloudFormation - AWS Prescriptive Guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/patterns/configure-bedrock-invocation-logging-cloudformation.html)

A healthcare company is building an AI application that retrieves medical literature to support doctors' research. The company plans to deploy this application across multiple countries. The application must index 50,000 text-heavy medical documents containing specialized terminology in English, French, and German, and it must deliver high search accuracy for that medical terminology. The company wants a solution requiring minimal custom code development and minimal ongoing maintenance.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon Titan Text Embeddings to process all documents in their original language without translation. Apply semantic chunking at the medical section level to preserve medical terminology context and to maintain moderate vector dimensions.
Use Amazon Titan Text Embeddings to translate all non-English documents to English before processing. Implement document chunking strategies based on logical sections to improve retrieval accuracy.
Use Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings to convert document pages to images. Generate text captions for the images to create a multimodal knowledge base that handles medical content.

Use an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base as the vector store. Use Amazon Kendra to perform multilingual document processing. Configure the vector store to automatically handle language detection and translation for each query.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Titan Text Embeddings natively supports over 100 languages, so it can generate high-quality embeddings directly from documents in their original language (English, French, or German) without a separate translation step, preserving the precise meaning of specialized medical terminology that could otherwise be lost or altered during translation. Applying semantic chunking at the medical section level keeps related terminology and context together, improving retrieval accuracy for domain-specific searches, while also controlling vector size (moderate dimensions) for efficient storage and query performance. This approach avoids extra translation pipelines, image-conversion workflows, or non-existent automatic in-store translation features, keeping custom development and ongoing maintenance to a minimum, consistent with AWS guidance on using Titan Text Embeddings for multilingual RAG and semantic search scenarios.

**Learn more:** [Amazon Titan Text Embeddings models - Amazon Bedrock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/titan-embedding-models.html) · [Get started with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/get-started-with-amazon-titan-text-embeddings-v2-a-new-state-of-the-art-embeddings-model-on-amazon-bedrock/)

A publishing company is building a chat assistant powered by a containerized large language model (LLM) that runs on Amazon SageMaker AI. The architecture includes an Amazon API Gateway REST API that forwards user requests to an AWS Lambda function, which in turn invokes a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint hosting the LLM.  
  
Users are experiencing inconsistent response times. Analytics reveal that many chats are abandoned after users wait 2 seconds for the first token to appear. The company needs a solution that keeps p95 latency under 800 ms for interactive requests to the chat assistant.  
  
Which combination of solutions will meet this requirement? (Choose two.)

options.text: Enable model preload upon container startup. Implement dynamic batching to process multiple user requests together in a single inference pass.
Select a larger GPU instance type for the SageMaker AI endpoint. Set the minimum number of instances to 0. Continue to perform per-request processing. Lazily load model weights on the first request.
Switch to a multi-model endpoint. Use lazy loading without request batching.
Set the minimum number of instances to greater than 0. Enable response streaming.
Switch to Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Inference for all requests. Store requests in an Amazon S3 bucket. Set the minimum number of instances to 0.

questions.explanation: Keeping the SageMaker AI real-time endpoint's minimum instance count above zero prevents cold-start delays caused by scaling from zero, ensuring an inference-ready instance is always available to handle requests immediately. Enabling response streaming allows the endpoint to return generated tokens incrementally as they are produced instead of waiting for the entire response to complete, which directly reduces the time-to-first-token that is causing users to abandon chats. Preloading the model at container startup removes the delay of loading model weights on the first request, which is a major contributor to inconsistent, high initial latency; combined with batching multiple concurrent requests efficiently, this keeps inference passes fast and consistent. Together, warm always-on capacity with streaming responses and pre-warmed model containers address both the cold-start and time-to-first-byte issues driving the poor p95 latency, while asynchronous inference, multi-model endpoints with lazy loading, and scale-to-zero configurations all introduce additional delay unsuitable for sub-second interactive chat requirements.

A company operates a generative AI application that uses multiple foundation models (FMs) from Amazon Bedrock to generate text. The application serves users across three AWS Regions and runs on AWS Lambda functions.  
  
The company needs to implement dynamic model selection based on response quality and latency metrics. The company must be able to switch between models without modifying or redeploying the application code. The company wants to gradually roll out new models, starting with 20% of traffic. The company also needs a solution that will automatically roll back if error rates exceed 1%.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS AppConfig to create feature flags for model selection criteria. Set up validation rules for error rates. Implement the AWS AppConfig Agent Lambda extension to retrieve model configurations when the functions run. Define linear deployment strategies to gradually release new models, starting with 20% of traffic.

Store model selection configurations in Amazon DynamoDUse global tables to enable multi-Region replication. Configure Amazon EventBridge rules to monitor Amazon CloudWatch metrics for errors and invoke AWS Lambda functions that update the DynamoDB table with model preferences. Add custom code to the Lambda functions to query DynamoDB before each model invocation.

Create Lambda function versions for each model configuration. Use Lambda aliases and set up routing configurations to gradually shift traffic between versions, starting with 20% of traffic. Implement AWS CodeDeploy deployments that monitor Amazon CloudWatch metrics for the Lambda function versions to automatically roll back deployments when error rales exceed thresholds.

Create Amazon CloudWatch dashboards to monitor response quality and latency metrics. Implement custom logic in the Lambda functions to select models based on metric thresholds. Use environment variables that are stored in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to define model selection parameters that can be updated across Regions.

questions.explanation:
AWS AppConfig lets you manage model-selection settings as feature flags that Lambda functions retrieve at runtime through the AWS AppConfig Agent Lambda extension, which polls for updated configuration data over a local HTTP endpoint, so no code changes or redeployments are needed to change which Bedrock model is used. AppConfig deployment strategies support a Linear growth type, where you define a growth factor (percentage of targets that receive the new configuration at each step, e.g., 20%) and a deployment duration, giving the required staged rollout starting at 20% of traffic. AppConfig also supports validators and CloudWatch alarm-based automatic rollback: if a configured CloudWatch alarm (such as one tracking error rate crossing a 1% threshold) enters the ALARM state during the deployment or the subsequent bake time, AppConfig automatically reverts the configuration to the last-known-good version, preventing continued exposure to a faulty model configuration. This combination of feature flags, Lambda extension retrieval, linear deployment strategy, and alarm-triggered rollback is documented in the AWS AppConfig user guide and directly satisfies every stated requirement, which the other options (custom DynamoDB/EventBridge logic, Lambda version/alias traffic shifting via CodeDeploy, or manual CloudWatch/Parameter Store logic) do not fully provide without extra custom engineering or without violating the no-redeploy requirement.

**Learn more:** [Working with deployment strategies - AWS AppConfig](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appconfig/latest/userguide/appconfig-creating-deployment-strategy.html) · [Monitoring deployments for automatic rollback - AWS AppConfig](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appconfig/latest/userguide/monitoring-deployments.html)

A financial services company is building an AI-powered search assistant to help investment advisors quickly retrieve investment data. The application runs as an AWS Lambda function and uses Amazon Bedrock, specifically an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base backed by Amazon OpenSearch Serverless as its data source.  
  
The application agent must manage collections at scale by automatically assigning access permissions to collections and indexes that match a specific pattern.  
  
While testing the knowledge base with Amazon Bedrock tools, the knowledge base sync process completes successfully. However, testing reveals:  
  
- A 400 Bad Authorization error from the BedrockAgentRuntime API  
- A 403 Forbidden error when attempting to access OpenSearch Serverless  
  
The company needs to resolve these permissions issues.  
  
Which combination of solutions will meet this requirement? (Choose two.)

options.text: Update the Lambda function execution role to include the bedrock:InvokeAgent permission. Add the aoss:APIAccessAll permission to the Lambda execution role.
Create an OpenSearch Serverless data access policy that includes pattern-based resource rules.
Configure a VPC endpoint policy for OpenSearch Serverless. Add the endpoint to the Lambda function’s VPC configuration.
Configure AWS Secrets Manager to store OpenSearch Serverless credentials. Grant the Lambda function access to retrieve the credentials.
Enable IAM authentication for the OpenSearch Serverless domain. Add the es:ESHttp* permission to the Lambda function execution role.

questions.explanation:
The Lambda function's IAM execution role must include bedrock:InvokeAgent so it is authorized to call the BedrockAgentRuntime API (resolving the 400 Bad Authorization error), and it must also include aoss:APIAccessAll, since AWS OpenSearch Serverless requires this specific IAM permission on top of any data access policy grants — without it, callers receive 403 Forbidden errors when accessing collections. Separately, OpenSearch Serverless data access policies natively support pattern-based (prefix + wildcard) resource rules for both collection and index resource types, which is exactly how AWS enables managing access at scale by automatically applying permissions to any new or existing collections/indexes whose names match a defined pattern. VPC endpoint policies address network path access rather than these authorization/authentication errors, Secrets Manager is not used for OpenSearch Serverless credentials since it relies on IAM-based auth, and es:ESHttp* permissions apply to standard (non-serverless) OpenSearch domains rather than OpenSearch Serverless collections.

**Learn more:** [Data access control for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/latest/developerguide/serverless-data-access.html) · [Create a service role for Amazon Bedrock Agents](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-permissions.html)
